label: Constitutional Analysis
sentences: The question here falls under Article I, Section 1. The lawmaking powers the Constitution grants are given to Congress, which is a Senate and a House. It reads: “All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.”
This story is about who may set new rules for bringing goods into the country.

In 1794, the joint resolution of March 26, 1794 provided "that the President of the United States be authorized to give such instructions to the revenue officers of the United States, as shall appear best adapted for carrying the said resolution into full effect."

In 1804, in Little v. Barreme (1804) the Court held that executive instructions "cannot change the nature of the transaction, or legalize an act which without those instructions would have been a plain trespass," and that Captain Little was liable in damages for seizing a neutral vessel.
The document sets new requirements for foreign importers of record.
The document sets responsibilities for licensed customs brokers.
The new rules set consequences for those who do not comply.
The strongest argument against this is that Congress can leave enforcing of revenue and customs work to officers who carry trade measures into effect.
We read this clause to mean binding requirements are rules of conduct that stay with Congress alone.
We read this clause to mean that executive direction cannot legalize what statute has not allowed.
This keeps the people’s elected lawmakers in charge of the rules.
